```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
has_glmmTMB <- requireNamespace("glmmTMB", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(isoniche)
```

This vignette covers the decisions to make before estimating niche breadth:
the data format, sampling effort, what counts as a replicate, which
habitats to include, and what to do with incomplete or small sites.

## Long format

All the main functions (`check_coverage()`, `fit_isodars()`,
`niche_breadth()`, `group_sites()`) take data in long format, with one row
per species x site x habitat and columns named by arguments:

| argument | column | required |
|---|---|---|
| `species` | species name | no (without it the data are one species) |
| `site` | replicate (site, or survey) | yes |
| `habitat` | habitat | yes |
| `abundance` | number of individuals | yes |
| `effort` | sampling effort | no (default: 1 for every row) |

Rules:

* A habitat not sampled at a site has no row. A habitat sampled where the
  species was not found has a row with abundance 0. If any species has a row
  for a site and habitat, that site and habitat count as sampled, and missing
  rows of other species there are treated as 0.
* There is at most one row per species, site and habitat; pool repeated
  samples first (see below).
* Sites where a species has no individuals at all are dropped for that
  species: they carry no information on how it distributes among habitats.
* If `habitat` is a factor, its levels set the order of habitats.

## From a community matrix

Community data are often stored as a matrix of samples x species, with a
separate table of sample attributes. `community_to_long()` converts them,
pooling samples from the same site and habitat and summing their effort:

```{r community}
comm <- matrix(c(12, 0, 3,
                  8, 2, 0,
                  5, 1, 1,
                  0, 5, 9,
                  2, 7, 4),
               nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(NULL, c("sp_a", "sp_b", "sp_c")))
samples <- data.frame(site = c("north", "north", "north", "south", "south"),
                      habitat = c("reef", "reef", "lagoon", "reef", "lagoon"),
                      area_m2 = c(100, 50, 100, 100, 100),
                      lon = c(-149.80, -149.80, -149.80, -149.85, -149.85),
                      lat = c(-17.48, -17.48, -17.48, -17.55, -17.55))
long <- community_to_long(comm, samples, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
                          effort = "area_m2", keep = c("lon", "lat"))
long
```

The result goes straight into the other functions, e.g.
`niche_breadth(long, species = "species", site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
abundance = "abundance", effort = "area_m2")`. Without an `effort` column,
each sample has effort 1, so pooled cells have effort equal to their number
of samples.

## Effort and the unit of abundance

Isodars relate *densities*, so counts are divided by effort: density =
abundance / effort. Effort can be area, transect length (with constant
width), trap nights or any relative measure, as long as it is the same kind
of measure in every row.

Densities are then expressed per `reference_effort`, by default the median
effort of the data. This is the sampling unit in which "one individual" and
all reported abundances (spillover abundance, the x-axis of niche breadth
curves) are measured. DI niche breadth is evaluated where the least
favoured habitat holds one individual per reference effort, so **DI niche
breadth and spillover abundance depend on this unit, while isodar slopes
and DD niche breadth do not**. Use the same `reference_effort` for all
species you compare, and report it.

```{r effort}
fish <- moorea_fish[moorea_fish$species == "Chaetodon ornatissimus", ]
fish$effort <- 1
unit1 <- niche_breadth(fish, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
                       abundance = "abundance", effort = "effort",
                       n_boot = 0, diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))
unit2 <- niche_breadth(fish, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
                       abundance = "abundance", effort = "effort",
                       reference_effort = 2, n_boot = 0,
                       diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))
data.frame(reference_effort = c(1, 2),
           rbind(unit1[c("nb_di", "spillover_abundance", "nb_dd")],
                 unit2[c("nb_di", "spillover_abundance", "nb_dd")]))
```

With `reference_effort = 2`, abundances are counted per two sampling units,
so "one individual" in the least-favoured habitat is reached later along the
isodars: the spillover abundance roughly doubles and DI niche breadth
changes, while DD niche breadth is unchanged.

## Replicates: sites or surveys

Isodars are estimated across replicates that differ in abundance. A
replicate can be a site, or one survey (a year, a season) of a site; put
its identifier in the `site` column. With several sites surveyed
repeatedly, each site x survey can be a replicate (combine the two into one
identifier), but repeated surveys of a site are not independent, and the
bootstrap, which resamples replicates, will then give intervals that are too
narrow. Pooling surveys within a site, or analysing years at a single site,
avoids this.

## Which habitats

Include the habitats *available* to the species: those it could reach. A
habitat the species never uses lowers its niche breadth, so species
compared with each other should be assessed over the same set of habitats.
Rare or poorly sampled habitats can be merged with similar ones before the
analysis.

## Absent and undersampled habitats

A habitat in which a species was never recorded is treated in one of two
ways:

* **absent**, when the habitat was sampled at enough sites where the species
  occurred (`absent_min_sites`, default 5) and the species was found there no
  more than `absent_max_count` times (default 0). It is fixed at 0, excluded
  from the isodar fit and counted as 0 in niche breadth.
* **undersampled**, when it was sampled at too few such sites. The zeros may
  then be chance, so the habitat is kept and the species is flagged.

```{r absent}
cov <- check_coverage(moorea_fish, species = "species", site = "site",
                      habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
cov[cov$species == "Chromis viridis", ]
```

The rule can be changed (`absent_max_count`, `absent_min_sites`), switched
off (`absent = "none"`) or replaced by naming the absent habitats
(`absent = "outer_slope"`), in `niche_breadth()` and `fit_isodars()`.

A habitat used at low abundance but predicted to be empty at high abundance
is *not* absent: it counts for DI niche breadth and is listed in the
`abandoned` column of `niche_breadth()`.

## Incomplete sites

Not every habitat needs to be sampled at every site. Pairwise isodars
(the default, `dim = "pairwise"`) use every site where both habitats of a
pair were sampled. The n-dimensional isodar (`dim = "ndim"`) can use sites
with at least two habitats through a one-factor model (`ndim_method =
"latent"`, needs the **glmmTMB** package); with `ndim_method = "auto"` it is
chosen whenever some sites are incomplete.

```{r latent, eval = has_glmmTMB}
set.seed(1)
inc <- simulate_isodars(slopes = c(1.5, 1, 0.8), intercepts = c(5, 0, 2),
                        n = 60, p_missing = 0.3, format = "long")
head(inc)
niche_breadth(inc, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
              abundance = "abundance", dim = "ndim", n_boot = 0,
              diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))[c("method", "n_sites", "nb_di",
                                                "nb_dd", "flags")]
```

## Grouping nearby sites

When single sites lack habitats or hold few individuals, nearby sites can
be merged into larger sampling units with `group_sites()`. It uses complete
linkage on great-circle distance, so every pair of sites in a group lies
within the radius; counts and efforts are summed.

```{r group}
set.seed(2)
d <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, n = 30, p_missing = 0.3,
                      format = "long")
xy <- data.frame(site = unique(d$site), lon = stats::runif(30, 0, 0.1),
                 lat = stats::runif(30, 0, 0.1))
d <- merge(d, xy)
g <- group_sites(d, site = "site", lon = "lon", lat = "lat", radius_km = 2,
                 habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
head(g)
```

The radius is not chosen automatically: choosing it to improve the results
would be circular. Instead, `radius_sensitivity()` shows how the number of
units, their completeness and the estimates change with the radius; choose
a radius on ecological grounds (e.g. the scale of movement of the species)
and check that the conclusions do not hinge on it:

```{r radius}
radius_sensitivity(d, site = "site", lon = "lon", lat = "lat",
                   habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance",
                   radii_km = c(0, 2, 5), diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))
```

`radius_km` can also be a named vector with one radius per species.

## One species in wide format

For a single species, data can also be given in wide format, one row per
site and one column per habitat (`NA` for habitats not sampled), with the
habitat columns named in `hab_cols`:

```{r wide}
set.seed(1)
sim <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, noise = 1, n = 30)
head(sim)
niche_breadth(sim, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3"), n_boot = 0,
              diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))[c("nb_di", "nb_dd")]
```

The lower-level functions `iai()` and `isoderr()` work on fitted isodars of
one species in this format; see their help pages.
